blocks.markdown: PDIC powers and payment — objectives: use the distressed-bank tools (financial assistance, examination, sanctions), trace closure → takeover → liquidation, run the payment and subrogation rules, and route every dispute to the right court and deadline.

PDIC acts in sequence, not simultaneously. **Before closure** (bank distressed but open), it is supervisor-rescuer: risk evaluation (Sec. 6), deposit-records examination (Sec. 11), sanctions escalation (Sec. 8), and financial assistance (Sec. 22(e)). **At closure** (MB order), it becomes receiver (Sec. 12), takes over (Sec. 14), and liquidates (Secs. 13-16) while paying insured deposits (Secs. 19, 21) and stepping into depositors' shoes (Sec. 20). Keep the two phases apart: assistance and sanctions belong to phase one; takeover, payout, and distribution belong to phase two.

Rescue before closure: PDIC may **lend, buy assets, assume liabilities, or place deposits** to save a bank in danger of closing — but only through a qualified investor or merger, only when cheaper than payoff-plus-liquidation (or on the systemic track with MB concurrence).

Scenario: a rural bank — the only bank in a farming town — is failing, and a stronger bank offers to acquire it. PDIC may assist the ACQUIRER or the merged institution (loans, asset purchases, liability assumptions, deposits) because community banking service is at stake — but first it must find that rescue costs less than paying all depositors and liquidating. If instead the MB finds SYSTEMIC consequences looming, PDIC may fund the bank directly to prevent failure, with MB concurrence and no added DIF cost at grant. Limits to remember: no buying the bank's voting/common stock (equity-form assistance only with Board + MB approval, sold off ASAP), and every grant needs the least-cost finding on record.
On MB-declared PCA failure **for capital deficiency**, PDIC and BSP may **open the deposit records** — a charter-carved exception to bank secrecy, with secrecy-law penalties for any leak.

The escalator: PDIC **examines and reports to the MB** → BSP issues the **cease-and-desist** → 30 days of defiance lets PDIC **terminate insured status** (final on publication, with a 180-day runoff for existing balances).

Do not conflate the two endings. **Termination of insured status** (Sec. 8): the bank keeps operating but WITHOUT insurance — old balances keep runoff cover for 180 days, new money is uninsured, and the bank must not claim otherwise. **Closure** (Sec. 12): the bank STOPS operating and PDIC takes over for liquidation. Between them sits examination (Sec. 9 Eighth / Sec. 11): fraud or unsafe-banking findings let PDIC look through RA 1405/RA 6426/RA 8791 secrecy, jointly with BSP. Exam sequence to memorize: examine → report → BSP order → 30-day cure → terminate (runoff) or, on graver grounds, MB closure.
The closure chain in one sentence: **MB closure order → PDIC is designated receiver → takeover → liquidation — and a closed bank is NEVER rehabilitated.**

Takeover mechanics: **serve the notice** (on the top officer present, or post it) — closure bites at that moment — then **take over**, while insiders holding bank assets **in trust** must immediately account, surrender, and inform.

The receiver needs **nobody's consent** to pick conventional liquidation, purchase-and-assumption, or both — then gathers, converts (including **FISTC bulk sales**), sues, collects and restructures loans, trims unreasonable rates, and distributes under concurrence-and-preference, with **surplus dividends at the legal rate** before stockholders see anything.

Liquidation freezes the bank: **corporation survives only to wind up (never reopens)**; **insiders lose all power and pay**; **assets enter custodia legis** (no attachment/garnishment/execution); **all employment ends** (separation pay ranked by preference); **interest stops at closure**.

blocks.markdown: The court track: an **in rem** petition for assistance in the RTC (exclusive over disputed claims) plus the twin **60-day clocks** — all claims to the receiver within 60 days from closure-notice publication (late = disallowed), denied claims to the liquidation court within 60 days from final denial.

Keep the two claims tracks apart — examiners mix them deliberately. **Track 1 — INSURANCE (depositor vs PDIC)**: determination starts at takeover with 3-week publication (Sec. 21(a)); PDIC pays cash or transferred deposit (Sec. 19); unpaid-withheld portions follow stockholder/loan setoff (Sec. 21(d)); claim within 2 years + enforce within 2 more (Sec. 21(e)); Sec. 5(g) denials go to the CA by certiorari in 30 days. **Track 2 — LIQUIDATION (creditor vs estate)**: all claims to the receiver in 60 days (Sec. 16(l)); denials to the liquidation court in 60 days; distribution by concurrence-and-preference; surplus dividends at legal rate; 6-month winding-up claim window; unclaimed assets to the Bureau of Treasury. Different clocks, different respondents, different courts.

Pay **as soon as possible** in **cash or transferred deposit**; PDIC may demand proof of claim or await a court ruling on doubtful claims — but culpable delay beyond **6 months** from filing jails the responsible officers (6 months to 1 year).

The insurance-claims machine: determination at **takeover** + **3-week publication**; proper payment **discharges**; PDIC may **withhold** for stockholder/loan liabilities; and the double **2-year bar** (claim, then enforce) ends the PDIC remedy while reverting the estate claim to the depositor.

Timeline a payout problem: **Day 0** — takeover; PDIC starts determining insured deposits and publishes notice weekly for 3 weeks. **Anytime within 2 years** — depositor files/claims with PDIC (proof of claim as required). **Within 6 months from filing** — PDIC must settle, or explain a genuine inter-agency legal/factual issue, or its officers risk jail. **Beyond 2+2 years** — PDIC remedy barred; only the estate claim (now reverted) survives. Withholding example: director-debtor Dana owes the bank P3M on a loan and holds P1M in deposits — PDIC may withhold her payout pending determination of that liability instead of paying her first and chasing later.

Pay and step in: PDIC is **subrogated** to the depositor's rights **up to the amount paid** (dividends + stockholder recoveries); the depositor keeps the **uninsured excess with the SAME preference**; payouts are **public funds = Art. 2244(9) preferred credit**.

Worked example (2025 closure, P1M MDIC): Lena is owed P2.5M. PDIC pays P1M and is subrogated for P1M; Lena keeps a P1.5M uninsured claim ranked EQUALLY with PDIC's. In liquidation both outrank ordinary unsecured creditors under Art. 2244(9). Accounting intuition: PDIC's payout is not a gift — it buys a preferred seat at the distribution table, which is how the DIF recovers part of what it pays out.

PDIC's litigation shield: **only the CA** may enjoin charter actions; the **Supreme Court** may do so only for extremely urgent constitutional issues with bond; any other injunction is **void** and suspends the issuing judge **60+ days without pay**.

**Trap: the RTC can do nothing against PDIC here.** A depositor who files certiorari vs a claim denial in the RTC (like So and Chugani first did) gets dismissed for lack of jurisdiction — PDIC is quasi-judicial, so Rule 65 petitions belong exclusively to the CA, within 30 days from denial. Likewise, an RTC TRO against a takeover, payout, or denial is void on its face. When a problem routes PDIC litigation to the RTC, the answer is dismissal/voidness, not merits.

**Exam point — the PDIC deadline ladder:** 30 days (CA certiorari vs Sec. 5(g) denial; BSP-order cure before status termination) → 60 days (claims to receiver; denied claims to liquidation court; reconsideration on new evidence) → 6 months (PDIC claim settlement; winding-up claim windows) → 180 days (runoff after status termination; suspension of pending actions) → 2+2 years (insurance-claim bar). Attach the right court to each: CA, receiver/RTC-liquidation-court, PDIC, PDIC.
